## Overview

Setos are an indigenous Finnic people and linguistic minority who have historically lived in the borderlands between modern-day Estonia and Russia. Their ancestral homes are south of Lake Peipus, in the Setomaa region, which after 1991 was divided between Estonia’s Põlva and Võro counties and the north-western sections of the Russian Federation’s Pskov Oblast. The Seto language belongs to the Finnic group of the Uralic language family. A 2011 census recorded nearly 12,500 Seto-speaking people in Estonia, nearly two-thirds of whom lived outside the historically Seto regions. Setos have historically spoken Seto and been Orthodox Christians. Their polyphonic folk singing, *leelo*, was added to the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

Seto *leelo* is usually performed by women dressed in traditional clothing.

### Architecture

They state that the Pskovo-Pechersky Monastery in Petseri was an important religious and communal center for the Seto peoples and that the monastery owned much of the land and the Seto Churches in the region.

## Music & performance

*Leelo* is the Setos’ polyphonic style of folk singing. It is usually performed by women dressed in traditional clothing. In 2009, *leelo* was added to the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage. During the Seto Kingdom Day celebration, the winning lead singer of a *leelo* group receives the title Mother of Song.

The tradition is also connected with the preservation and study of Seto folk songs and traditional vocal polyphony. Paul Hagu, an ethnic Seto and a researcher of Seto folk songs and traditional vocal polyphony at the University of Tartu, initiated the tradition of choosing a steward of King Peko for the Kingdom of Setomaa.

## Festivals & rituals

The annual Day of the Kingdom, also called Seto Kuningriigi päiv, is a local festival that rotates among the bigger Seto villages. Every year, the Seto choose a steward of King Peko, called *sootska* or *ülebtsootska*, for the so-called Kingdom of Setomaa. The office is largely ceremonial and has been held by local activists, politicians, entrepreneurs, and scholars. During the celebration, the winning lead singer of a *leelo* group is awarded the title Mother of Song.

The Seto Congress, comprising representatives of Seto villages and organizations, is regularly convened every three years and elects a permanent Council of Elders. In 2002, at the sixth Seto Congress, the Setos declared their intent to identify as a separate people group.

Since 2007, Jumalamägi, described as God’s Hill and an ancient sacred grove dedicated to the God-King Peko, has again been a center of communal activity. Peko was believed to carry spirits to the afterlife in his horse wagon. A sculpture by the local sculptor R. Veeber was erected on the hill, which became an important location for offerings to Peko by the local community.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used mention Seto folk songs and traditional vocal polyphony. The Setomaa region’s folktales from the collection of Hendrik Prants are mentioned as an external resource, but the sources used do not summarize their contents.

Seto cultural and religious identity has been recreated in communities formed by people who migrated away from Setomaa. The Setomaa federation of municipalities publishes the newspaper Setomaa partly in the Seto language and partly in Estonian.

## Language & religion

Setos have historically spoken the Seto language, which belongs to the Finnic group of the Uralic language family, alongside Estonian and Finnish. Since the early 2000s, the Setos have sought greater recognition for Seto rather than having it considered a dialect of Estonian. Setos have historically been Orthodox Christians, and Eastern Orthodox Christianity, influenced by local folk religions, is widely practiced.

During the 13th century, many Estonians along the coasts were converted to Catholicism during the Livonian Crusade led by the Teutonic Order, while most Setos lived under the Novgorod Republic and remained followers of their native Finnic religion. Over the next two hundred years, Setos were converted to Orthodox Christianity under the influence of neighboring Slavic states while incorporating elements of their earlier pre-Christian religion.

The Pskovo-Pechersky Monastery in Petseri was an important religious and communal center. Elements of pre-Christian religion preserved during Christianization and Sovietization began to reemerge after the fall of the Soviet Union.
